Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 5:42pm

By Stephen Letts

That's it for another day on the blog, thanks for your company.

The equities global rally looks like continuing tonight with US and European futures trading pointing to gains of about 1-to-2%.

We'll be back bright and early tomorrow with all the news from overnight, right through the day and the RBA rates decision at 2:30pm AEST.

If you need a finance fix in the meantime, check out our Business Daily and FuelWatch podcacsts, and there's The Business with Kirsten Murray on ABC News at 8:44pm AEST and after the Late News on ABC TV.

Until next time, missing you already ...

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 5:39pm

By Stephen Letts

Relief for the global economy is in sight, with the re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz part of the terms of the US-Iran ceasefire deal.

The price of Brent crude dropped sharply on the news but it is still a way off its pre-war low of $US70 a barrel.

On truth social, US President Donald Trump wrote "let the oil flow".

Kevin Morrison from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis joins Kirsten Aiken on The Business to discuss how quickly that could happen.

Mr Morrison says the most recent fuel figures from the federal government show motorists used slightly less fuel during April.

Diesel figures experienced a spike in March most likely on the back of stockpiling and there were pronounced moves in aviation fuel usage as planes avoided the conflict zone.

As for ongoing fuel supplies, he says in the short term, it's going to be weeks before first flows of oil or gas are seen.

But it's probably going to be well into next year before supplies are back to pre-war levels.

That's The Business, 8:44pm (AEST) on ABC News and after the Late News on ABC TV.

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 5:23pm

By Stephanie Chalmers

Billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting has bought into Elon Musk's SpaceX, describing last week's stock market float as a "world leading IPO".

The Wall Street Journal reported the investment topped $US1 billion ($1.4b).

Rinehart, the executive chairman of Hancock, was effusive of Musk in announcing the stake, including lauding his role in DOGE.

"This is a significant investment for Hancock, and we are pleased to have received an allocation in what has been an extremely popular and oversubscribed IPO," she said.

"SpaceX is yet another clear example of why the world needs more enterprise, more builders and much less bureaucracy.

"It has delivered lower costs and greater capability by moving with the urgency and discipline that bureaucracy too often delays or prevents."

The move sees Hancock Prospecting move outside its typical industries of mining, particularly iron ore, and agriculture.

Hancock CEO Garry Korte said "the generous allocation of SpaceX shares was a strong endorsement" of Rinehart, who has had several meetings with Musk.

"In a heavily oversubscribed IPO, Hancock's allocation of SpaceX shares is a very pleasing result. It reflects the international regard for our chairman and company."

He said the company saw "the possibility of mutually beneficial arrangements between SpaceX and Hancock Prospecting's significant critical minerals investments, as demand grows for the materials and infrastructure needed to support advanced technology".

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:43pm

By Daniel Ziffer

In-the-gun consulting firm KPMG will not bid for more government work for the next three months, according to a Department of Finance note.

Important, but also redundant. The stink around its misuse of confidential client data means that for the next little while, it is going to be treated like PwC was in the wake of its "stuffing around with confidential data" scandal.

Attributable to a  spokesperson:

"KPMG Australia (KPMG) has agreed to the Department of Finance’s (Finance) request that KPMG will not bid for any new Commonwealth work until 30 September 2026.

"Between 16 June and 30 September 2026 KPMG will temporarily cease new contract engagements with Australian Government entities subject to the Commonwealth Procurement Rules (CPR), with non-CPR covered entities recommended to adopt a consistent approach.

"During this timeframe, Finance will commission an independent review of KPMG’s governance, culture, ethics and integrity frameworks. Further details regarding the review will be made available in due course."

This is big.

Inevitable, but big.

What a debacle for the firm, which has thousands of smart-as staff (and contracts) that have nothing to do with the problems in the audit division.

Those hearings on Friday are going to be blockbuster.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:42pm

By Stephen Letts

The ASX started the week strongly, supported by news of a ceasefire deal between the US and Iran and a corresponding fall in global oil prices.

At the close, the benchmark ASX 200 was up 1.3% to 8,914 points, while the broader All Ordinaries gained 1.4% to 9,128 points.

The miners in the materials sector led the way in a broad rally, while the oil and gas producers, energy-focused utilities (AGL -0.1% and Origin -3.3%) and supermarkets were out of favour.

The single stock education sector jump reflects IDP's 11.3% gain today.

Most of the big miners gained; BHP and Rio Tinto were up 3.6% and 2.7% respectively.

The copper-focused Capstone was in demand (+10.5%) supported by higher metal prices in this risk-on climate.

Only South 32 (-1.1%) went backwards.

Gold miners were the stellar performers. Vault Minerals was up about 15% and Newmont 7%.

Oil and gas producers were hammered. Karoon and Santos both fell 8.4% while Woodside shed 5.7% after dismissing media reports it was a takeover target.

However, at the other end of the oil pipeline, travel stocks relished the prospect of lower fuel prices and a Middle East ceasefire.

Virgin jumped almost 13%. Qantas and Flight Centre picked up 6.3% and 7.3% respectively

The banks were in demand; NAB up 2.6% and Judo Capital +3.8%.

However, insurers struggled. QBE fell 2.5%

Supermarkets were also out of favour. Coles shed 2.6%

The top movers list on the ASX 200 was dominated by gold miners.

Ora Banda led the way after signing a new production contract for its Davyhurst mine, north of Kalgoorlie.

The bottom movers list was populated by the fossil fuel brigade — oil and gas producers, fuel refiners (Viva -5.8% and Ampol -7.3%) and coal miners (New Hope -8.0%).

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:00pm

By Stephen Letts

As Swissquote's Ipek Ozkardeskaya pondered in her morning European note, is it the 40th time lucky for some sort of concrete peace deal?

"This time it could be real, as the Pakistani PM announced this weekend that the US and Iran had reached an agreement to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz by Friday.

"It was his first announcement [versus 39 announcements of a peace deal by US President Trump since the conflict began three months ago, according to Bloomberg]."

"As such, markets are taking the news seriously.

"US crude fell 4.5% in Asia to $80pb — by far the lowest level since the first days of the war — and global equities rallied with joy.

"The Nikkei rose nearly 3% to a fresh record high, while the Korean Kospi index rallied more than 5%, close to a record high.

"European and US futures are firmly in the green into the European open, as the decline in oil prices could prove sustainable and lead to easing inflation expectations globally, and a softer monetary policy stance across central banks.

"The US 2-year yield is down to 4% this morning, reflecting that thinking."

By Stephanie Chalmers

Wasn't KPMG being grilled today? Anything happening on that front? Have they been roasted or slightly seared?
Thanks

- Brad

Hi Brad, you're on the right track, just a few days ahead of yourself.

A joint parliamentary committee will hold hearings into KPMG in Canberra, from 8:15am AEST this Friday.

And it could be a long day — it's slated for a 6:30pm finish, but with more than 30 witnesses to appear, including senior leadership from the accounting firm, it could run over.

KPMG is engulfed in a scandal that has resulted in several senior leaders quitting their roles and the corporate watchdog launching a formal investigation into the firm's business dealings.

It all centres on an internal whistleblower's allegations that some of the firm's senior partners misused confidential client documents.

We'll of course have full coverage and analysis here on the blog, so stay tuned.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 3:30pm

By Stephen Letts

We'll no doubt be hearing a lot more about the US government's order to Anthropic to disable access by foreign nationals to its top tier AI models.

The intervention comes at a delicate time for Anthropic as it positions itself for public float, expected to be one of the biggest in history similar to the rarified air occupied by SpaceX's $US2.1 trillion IPO on Friday.

The order suspends access to the company's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models by any foreign national—whether inside or outside the US, including Anthropic's own foreign employees.

IG Market's Tony Sycamore says the move will slash the amount of money Anthropic is likely to make when listed.

"This drastic step reportedly comes after researchers at Amazon used a series of prompts to bypass guardrails, forcing the Fable 5 model to provide restricted information that could be used to aid cyberattacks," Mr Sycamore said.

"In response — IG's Anthropic Pre-Market IPO valuation has dropped from about $US1.85 trillion down to $US1.72 trillion—a loss of $130 billion, or 7%."

By Stephen Letts

The big news up ahead is tomorrow's Reserve Bank meeting.

Spoiler alert: The official cash rate is expected to remain parked at 4.35%.

Reuters says its survey of 45 market economists found 42 are forecasting no change, given indications that the economy is starting to slow in response to the three successive rate hikes this year and a noticeable moderation in headline inflation.

Here's our guru-in-residence Alan Kohler with his take ahead of the meeting.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:48pm

By Stephen Letts

Iron ore futures are on the rise, as potential strikes at Australia's primary iron ore hub, Port Hedland, threatened to curb supply, while a preliminary U.S.-Iran agreement to end the conflict also lent support to metals.

The most-traded September iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE) gained 0.52% to $US113.94/tonne

The benchmark July iron ore on the Singapore Exchange was 0.7% higher at $US102.1/tonne

Iron ore inventories at major Chinese ports rose 0.75% to 160 million tonnes week-on-week, data from consultancy Steelhome showed.

Iron ore supply from Australia is expected to tighten due to an impending strike by BHP workers at Port Hedland in Western Australia this week, after voting in favour of a strike over better pay and working conditions.

One union said last Thursday, around 100 members endorsed work stoppages ranging from 30 minutes to 24 hours.

In addition, optimism surrounding the end of the Iran war after the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the US blockade of Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz resulted in a rally in metals.

Other steelmaking ingredients on the DCE were mixed, with coking coal down 2.1% and coke 0.9%, respectively.

Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange gained.

Rebar was up 0.5%, hot-rolled coil advanced 0.56%, wire rod edged up 0.1% and stainless steel lifted 0.9%.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:31pm

By Political reporter Courtney Gould

University of Melbourne associate professor Kathryn James has appeared at the CGT Senate inquiry, and was asked if start-ups should be carved out of the proposed changes to the capital gains discount.

The sector is concerned because of a low-cost base (say a laptop at someone's kitchen table) means there is little purchase price to index to inflation, so investors lose a much greater tax benefit than traditional companies.

But James says once you start making exemptions it snowballs, and having a broad tax base is simpler.

"To me, it's defensible that if you've ... sold a profitable business then a tax of 30 per cent, once you've been able to deduct your losses, is reasonable and defensible," she said.

"Once we start introducing carve outs for certain sectors and certain industries then we can see what's happening in relation to this Senate committee ... everyone can make a claim case for special treatment, and it starts to snowball."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:35pm

By Daniel Ziffer

Interesting analysis of last week's radio figures, from global radio guru and host of Podnews, James Cridland.

We were all understandably focused on the smashing fall-out of the end of shockjocks Kyle and Jackie O and the impact on listed company ARN, which both wrote the failed $200m deal to keep them and seen its share price drop more than 80% in the past five years.

Anyway, Cridland made the good observation that listeners haven't deserted radio, but they haven't found one new home either.

"In Sydney, as you might guess, breakfast on KIIS has nose-dived, from an average quarter-hour audience of 91,000 (S3 2025) to just 62,000 (S3 2026). This has led to no end of confident deskjockeys on LinkedIn, claiming that people have just switched the radio off.

"That’s actually not the case.

"The total Sydney breakfast radio audience is up by 3% year-on-year. More people listening to the radio, year-on-year. Not less people.

"Incidentally, total average quarter hours (AQH, how listening is measured in surveys) ought to increase year-on-year: Sydney’s population is growing by about 1.2% every year. But this is an increase of twice that.

"In fact, the total AQH for Sydney breakfast, 652,000, is exactly the same as S1 2026, when Kyle Sandilands was peddling his particularly puerile piss-poor prattle. Interesting that KIIS’s audience hasn’t found an obvious natural home elsewhere, though — it’s been spread between the other commercial music stations.

"Comparing S1 to S3, Triple M is up from 39,000 to 48,000; GOLD is up from 47,000 to 55,000; Smooth is up from 78,000 to 86,000; and NOVA is up from 65,000 to 72,000.

"In fact, the one station you’d expect to win, 2DAY, has lost audience."

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:12pm

By Stephen Letts

It's never a good look when a stock market regulator admits to breaching its own regulations and misleading its own shareholders, but here we are with the ASX.

It's now facing a $20.5 million fine and well as footing the $3 million legal bill of fellow regulator ASIC, which hauled it into the Federal Court for making misleading statements in 2022 that its replacement project for the outdated CHESS settlement platform was on track.

It wasn't — it was an expensive hi-tech train wreck that was ultimately scrapped and will now be replaced with a cheaper off-the-shelf product sometime in the future.

The cost to the ASX is also reputational.

ASX chair David Clarke apologised for the mess this morning noting, "when we stopped the CHESS project in November 2022 to reassess our whole approach, that tested market confidence in ASX and called into question the nature of statement previously made.

"As the market operator and a steward of critical market infrastructure, our words matter."

Well, yes, they do — not only to the broader Australian stock market and investor community, but particularly to ASX shareholders — the company's owners.

Those most aggrieved are investors who ploughed there "hard-earned" into ASX between the "everything is on track" statement on February 20, 2022 and the price crunching, "Ooops, no they're not — we need a plan B" statement in November.

It's that sort of misdirection that has made lawyers and litigation funders very well wealthy and aggrieved shareholders marginally better off than they were.

So, the ASX SNAFU looks like fertile ground for the lawyers and yet another cost on top of the $23.5 million the regulator is already on the hook for.

However, J.P. Morgan analyst and respected ASX watcher Siddharth Parameswaran is not so sure saying today's settlement may have a "silver lining" for ASX and there is now only a "very modest risk" of a class action by shareholders.

"Whilst the full wording of the settlement has not been released (usually is tabled when the final court agreement is reached), it appears to us prima facie that (1) given the ASX has always maintained that they believe they had a strong legal case to defend against the proceedings, and their desire to improve regulatory relations (without exposing excessive financial risk) … we think there is only very modest risk of a shareholder class action (one of the key risks we have been worried about)," Mr Parameswaran wrote in a note to clients.

Mr Parameswaran also noted it appeared now there were only around seven weeks of trading where the market may have been misinformed, which may help beat off a class action.

"Overall, it appears to us that the current board is still in "clean-up" mode before the arrival of the new CEO Anthony Attia," he said.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:01pm

By Stephen Letts

The ceasefire deal and hopes that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen is dominating global markets today and is driving down oil prices.

But there are still a lot of questions about whether oil (or around 20% of global supply that has been locked in) will really start to flow again, when will fuel supplies normalise again and what next for oil prices?

Carrington Clarke and our roving finance guru Alan Kohler give these questions and plenty more a decent thrashing in the latest edition of our Fuelcast podast.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 12:15pm

By Political reporter Courtney Gould

Political reporter Courtney Gould here from Canberra, listening into the two-day Senate hearing into the proposed changes to capital gains tax discount and negative gearing.

Matt Grudnoff, senior economist at The Australia Institute, told senators while property prices would moderate it's possible prices for new builds will increase as "investors compete in order to buy them".

"Now if newer prices go up faster than existing properties then builders are going to want to supply more of those because they will be the profitable things to do."

Greg Jericho, chief economist at the Australia Institute, when asked about recent auction clearance rates, says he thinks potential buyers are currently just waiting to what happens with the legislation.

If prices do experience a drop (he mentioned some reports of a 10% decrease) then that would take house prices back to December 2024 levels: "Which I don't think anyone was suggesting that was a real cheap time to buy".

When asked about young people and the CGT and investments (say through an EFT or something similar), Grudnoff argued that he didn't think young people would notice the extra tax paid.

"The vast majority of them will probably pay no more tax, and the small amount that do probably won't notice the increase in tax, but what they will notice is house prices remaining flat. They will notice that as their incomes rise every year, housing becomes more and more affordable."
